topic: framing and straightening the roof of a small timber workshop

provenance.author: subagent-en-b
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is measurement arithmetic and cutting lists with closed task questions, base is a diagnostic conversation about a sagging ridge. Grounded external referent: the scaffold, introduced in turn 0 as the datum the ridge was set out from and carried through the whole diagnosis (it settles under the tile stacks, the props stand on its deck, the final check has to come off it).

a: Here are six rafters cut for the workshop roof, measured this morning with a steel tape.
The first three run three point one, two point eight and three point four metres.
The other three run three point one, two point nine and three point three metres.
Sort them from longest to shortest, and convert every length into millimetres.
Mark the ones that differ from three point two metres and give the mean length.
How many millimetres separate the longest rafter from the shortest one on that list?
base: We are framing a roof over the workshop and the ridge line is visibly out of true.
The building is six metres long and the scaffold runs along both sides at eaves height.
We set the ridge out from the scaffold deck and it sags perhaps twenty millimetres in the middle.
All the rafters came from the same batch of timber and were cut on the same day.
What would you check first before we start packing anything out with shims?

a: Longest to shortest gives three point four, then three point three, then three point one twice.
The last two are two point nine and two point eight metres along the top edge.
In millimetres the list starts at three thousand four hundred and three thousand three hundred.
Every rafter differs from three thousand two hundred millimetres, so all six take a mark.
The mean of the six comes out at three thousand one hundred millimetres.
Does the extreme difference of six hundred millimetres match the cutting sheet?
base: Start with the wall plates again, because a spirit level over six metres hides a great deal.
Run a taut string from end to end and measure down to the plate every metre.
Do not take that measurement off the scaffold deck, which settles under the tile stacks.
Check the birdsmouth cuts too, since a deep seat cut drops that rafter by its own depth.
Are the birdsmouths all cut to the same depth, or were they marked one by one?

a: Next I need collar ties at one third of the rafter length down from the ridge.
Give that distance for each of the six rafters, rounded to the nearest five millimetres.
Then list the six ties from longest to shortest with their cut lengths in millimetres.
Each tie spans one point eight metres across at that height on every pair.
Which cut length does a tie take once fifty millimetres of overlap is added?
base: The birdsmouths were marked one at a time against the plate, by two different people.
That would explain a great deal, because nobody worked to one single set-out line.
We have no string line long enough, though there is a laser somewhere in the van.
The scaffold boards were our datum for everything, and the tiles arrived on them last week.
How much variation in seat depth would show up as twenty millimetres at the ridge?

a: One third down from the ridge is one thousand one hundred thirty-five millimetres for the longest.
The next two come out at one thousand one hundred and one thousand thirty-five millimetres.
The last three come out at one thousand thirty-five, nine hundred sixty-five and nine hundred thirty-five.
Every tie spans one point eight metres, so each cut length is one thousand eight hundred fifty millimetres.
Does one cut length of one thousand eight hundred fifty millimetres serve all six ties?
base: If the scaffold was your datum, then two of these problems are stacked on top of each other.
A seat cut two millimetres deep changes that rafter's height by the same two millimetres.
Twenty millimetres of sag is not seat depth alone, so something else is adding to it.
Look at the ridge board itself, which may well be sagging between its own supports.
What section is the ridge, and how many props are holding it at the moment?

a: Correction on the third rafter: it is three point zero five metres, not three point one.
Recalculate its millimetre length, its place in the sorted list and the new mean.
Leave the collar ties alone, since they do not depend on the rafter lengths.
Then give the total running metres of timber for all six rafters together.
How many whole metres does that total reach once ten percent of waste is added?
base: The ridge is a plain board, thirty-two by two hundred, with props at each end only.
Nothing holds it in the middle apart from the rafters that lean against it.
The props stand on the scaffold deck rather than on the workshop floor below.
Now that I look along it from the gable, the bow is obvious in daylight.
Would a single prop in the middle be enough to take that bow out?

a: Three point zero five metres is three thousand fifty millimetres, below both three thousand one hundred rafters.
It takes fourth place, ahead of two thousand nine hundred and two thousand eight hundred.
The new mean is eighteen thousand five hundred fifty divided by six, or three thousand ninety-two.
Total timber is eighteen point five five metres before any waste is added.
Does twenty-one metres cover the order once the ten percent is included?
base: A prop standing on the scaffold deck is worth very little, because the deck moves with it.
Thirty-two millimetres on edge is thin as well, and it carries thrust from both slopes.
Prop it from the workshop floor now, then sister a second board alongside.
Do the packing at the plates only after the ridge is straight and properly held.
Have you fixed the rafters at the ridge yet, or are they still nailed loosely?

a: Now the battens, which sit at three hundred fifty millimetre centres up each slope.
The slope length is two point eight metres from plate to ridge on both sides.
Tell me how many batten rows fit one slope and what distance is left at the top.
Each row is six metres long, so give the running metres of batten as well.
How many rows does the roof take once both slopes are counted?
base: The rafters are nailed at the ridge already, two skew nails into the board each side.
Pulling them off would take most of a day and probably split a few ends.
There is also the matter of the tiles, which are stacked on the scaffold now.
We wanted to load out this week while the weather is still holding dry.
Can the propping and sistering be done with the rafters left where they are?

a: Two thousand eight hundred divided by three hundred fifty gives exactly eight rows per slope.
There is no leftover distance, since the spacing divides the slope without a remainder.
Both slopes together therefore take sixteen rows from the plate up to the ridge.
At six metres a row, that is ninety-six running metres of batten for the roof.
Order in five metre lengths and allow roughly ten metres more for the joints.
base: Yes, all of it can be done from below with the rafters left in place.
Prop the ridge from the floor with an adjustable prop and a spreader on top.
Move the tile stacks off the scaffold first, because that load is bending the deck.
Then pack the plates where the string shows a dip, using slate or hardwood shims.
Do not load the tiles until the ridge line reads straight along its whole length.

a: Give a cutting list for the sistering board in three lengths that fit the van.
The board must total six metres, and the van takes nothing over two point five metres.
Use equal lengths where possible and give the joint positions along the ridge.
The props stand at zero and six metres, so keep the joints away from those points.
Which length does each of the three pieces take under that rule?
base: That order makes sense and the prop is already in the van from the last job.
The tiles will come down onto pallets so the scaffold deck is unloaded first.
The shims are the part I am least sure about, since slate can crush over time.
We have oak offcuts as well, though they are only about ten millimetres thick.
Which of the two would you use under a plate carrying the whole roof load?

a: Three pieces of two metres each give six metres and fit the van comfortably.
The joints then fall at two metres and four metres, clear of both props.
Piece one runs from zero to two metres, and piece two from two to four.
Piece three runs from four to six metres, finishing at the far prop position.
Stagger the bolts either side of each joint so no joint sits on one fixing.
base: Use the oak, cut into pads about a hundred millimetres square under each dip.
Slate is fine in thin single leaves but it splits once you stack several together.
Oak takes the load across the grain without crushing, which is what you want here.
Bed each pad on a little mortar so it seats evenly against the wall top.
Then check the string again from the ground rather than from the scaffold deck.
